title: Bank Mergers and Crime: The Real and Social Effects of Credit Market Competition
research_question: Do reductions in local credit market competition cause deterioration in local credit conditions, real economic activity, and demographic composition, and do these changes spill over into higher crime rates? Specifically, how does increased local banking concentration affect interest rates, loan availability, construction, property prices, household income composition, and property versus violent crime in affected neighborhoods?
data_description: The study combines several data sources at the neighborhood, county, and state levels. Property-level data come from COMPS.com and consist of 22,642 U.S. commercial real estate transactions from January 1992 to March 1999 across 11 states plus DC, including sale price, capitalization rate, property age, latitude/longitude coordinates, and detailed loan terms (interest rate, loan-to-value, maturity, amortization, lender identity). Bank merger and asset data come from the Federal Reserve's Commercial Bank Database and Call Reports, identifying 769 lenders (210 with at least $1 billion in assets). Crime risk scores at eight-digit lat/long coordinates for 1990, 1995, and 2000 come from CAP Index, Inc., supplemented by FBI Uniform Crime Reports at the county and state levels. Census tract data (1990 and 2000) provide income, unemployment, and home values; F.W. Dodge supplies county construction data; state branching deregulation dates are also used.
institutional_context: During the 1990s, the U.S. banking industry experienced extensive consolidation, with mergers and acquisitions among large commercial banks dominating changes in banking structure. Despite national integration of capital markets, commercial real estate lending—particularly for small loans—remains highly localized due to information and agency frictions, with surveys showing borrowers typically use lenders within roughly 4–15 miles. When two large banks combine, local loan markets where both previously operated become more concentrated, potentially raising borrowing costs and restricting credit until new entry or expanded lending by competitors restores competitive equilibrium (typically within about three years). Simultaneously, many states liberalized intra- and interstate branching restrictions during the 1970s–1990s, with several adopting unrestricted branching in the early-to-mid 1990s, providing additional variation in local banking competition. These institutional shifts created localized, plausibly exogenous changes in credit market competitiveness affecting neighborhoods of differing economic fragility.
